checks: Confirm the failure start time lines up with the most recent deployment window
Check whether ALL users are affected or only one group (e.g. one office or role)
Search the application log for 'authentication', 'LDAP', 'bind' and 'access denied' around the start time
Verify the authentication configuration (LDAP URL, bind account, SSO metadata) was not overwritten by the deployment
escalation: Escalate to the platform / identity team if the identity provider itself is down, and to the release manager if a rollback decision is needed. Page the incident lead when all users are locked out for more than 30 minutes.
steps: Reproduce the login with a test account and note the exact error message and timestamp
Compare the deployed authentication configuration against the last known-good version in source control
If the bind/service account password was rotated, update the encrypted credential store and restart the affected node
If SSO is used, re-check the identity-provider certificate expiry and clock skew between servers (keep skew under 5 minutes)
Validate login for one user from each affected group before declaring recovery
If the config diff cannot be fixed in place within 30 minutes, follow RB-106 (Deployment Rollback)
symptoms: Users see 'Invalid credentials' or a blank screen immediately after login
Failures start right after a deployment or configuration change
Login works in one environment (e.g. QA) but not in production
Application log shows LDAP / SSO bind errors or 'user not found' entries
title: Login & Authentication Failure After Deployment

checks: Check the slow-query log for claim-intake queries and note the top 3 by total time
Look for a recently added validation rule or integration call running synchronously on save
Check database locks: is one long transaction blocking claim inserts?
Compare today's intake volume with the 7-day average to rule out a genuine traffic spike
escalation: Escalate to the DBA team if slow queries persist after locks clear, and to the application lead if a code or rule change is needed. Raise to P1 if intake is effectively down at peak.
steps: Capture one slow request end-to-end (timestamp, user, claim type) so it can be found in the logs
If a blocking lock is found, identify the owning session and follow the change process before killing it
If a synchronous integration call is the bottleneck, confirm the downstream system health (see RB-103) before changing ClaimCenter
Temporarily raise the intake thread pool only if queue depth is growing and CPU has headroom; record the change for review
Re-test intake with the captured scenario and confirm save time is back under the normal threshold
symptoms: First Notice of Loss (FNOL) screens take more than 10 seconds to save
Adjusters report spinning / timeouts when creating a new claim
Slowness is worst at peak hours and improves off-peak
Server CPU is normal but response times keep climbing
title: Slow Claim Intake (FNOL) Performance

checks: Identify the exact endpoint and the timeout value from the integration log
Test connectivity from the app server to the endpoint (DNS, port, TLS handshake)
Check whether the downstream system is returning slowly or not at all (5xx vs no response)
Look for a message queue backlog building up behind the failing integration
escalation: Escalate to the integration owner and the downstream vendor/team if the endpoint is down. Page the incident lead if payments are blocked for more than 1 hour.
steps: Confirm the downstream system's status with its owning team before changing ClaimCenter settings
If messages are queued, leave them in place — do not purge; they should replay once the endpoint recovers
If the endpoint is healthy but slow, raise the read timeout one step (e.g. 30s to 60s) through the change process and monitor error rate
Verify a single test payment end-to-end after recovery, then watch the queue drain
Log the incident window so any duplicate-payment checks can be reconciled later
symptoms: Payment issuance fails with 'Read timed out' or 'Connection timed out' errors
Integration log shows repeated retries to the same endpoint
Claims themselves save fine — only the outbound call fails
Downstream status page may show degraded performance
title: Integration Timeout — Payment & External Services

checks: Open the job's run history: exact failure time, records processed, records failed
Read the FIRST error in the job log, not the last — later errors are usually knock-on effects
Check whether one bad record (data issue) or the whole job (infrastructure issue) failed
Verify the database and integration endpoints the job needs were up during the run window
escalation: Escalate to the application lead if the same job fails two nights in a row, and to the DBA team for repeated lock or space errors. Raise to P1 if a regulatory feed is missed.
steps: If a single bad record is identified, quarantine it per the data-fix process and note its claim/record ID
Re-run the job for the failed chunk only, if the job supports partial re-runs
Watch the re-run to completion and confirm record counts match expectations
If the failure was infrastructure (DB down, endpoint down), fix that first, then re-run the full job
Update the incident log with the root cause category: data, infrastructure, or code
symptoms: A scheduled batch job shows status FAILED in the morning check
Job log ends abruptly or shows the same record failing repeatedly
Downstream reports or feeds are missing the night's data
Job ran fine the previous night with no code change
title: Batch Job Failure (Nightly Jobs & Schedulers)

checks: Count active vs idle connections from the application on the database
Look for one query or batch job holding connections far longer than normal
Check for a connection leak pattern: steady climb in open connections with no plateau
Confirm the database itself is up and accepting connections from other clients
escalation: Escalate to the DBA team immediately if the database is rejecting connections from all clients. Page the incident lead — this is P1 while users are affected.
steps: If one runaway process is holding connections, stop that process first and watch the pool recover
Restart ONE application node and confirm it serves traffic cleanly before touching other nodes
Do not raise the pool size as a first fix — it masks leaks; only raise it as a temporary, logged change
Capture thread dumps and the top SQL statements during the incident for root-cause analysis
Monitor connection counts for at least 30 minutes after recovery before closing the incident
symptoms: Log shows 'Cannot get a connection' or 'Connection pool exhausted'
Errors appear across many screens at once, not just one feature
Application recovers briefly after a restart, then fails again
Database shows many idle or long-running sessions from the app server
title: Database Connection Errors & Pool Exhaustion

checks: Confirm the incident started with the deployment and no other change window overlaps
Check whether the release included a database schema change — schema changes may make rollback unsafe
Verify the previous version's artefacts and configuration are still available
Confirm the rollback decision owner (release manager / incident lead) has approved
escalation: Only the incident lead or release manager can approve a rollback. Escalate to them immediately when fix-forward is estimated over 60 minutes during a P1.
steps: Announce the rollback in the incident channel with the start time and expected duration
Stop incoming traffic / enable the maintenance page if the platform supports it
Redeploy the previous known-good artefact version to one node and smoke-test login and claim search
Restore the previous configuration set from source control; re-check secrets and endpoints
Roll the remaining nodes, then run the standard post-deployment smoke tests
Keep the failed version's logs and artefacts untouched for root-cause analysis
symptoms: A new release causes P1 errors that cannot be fixed forward quickly
Error rate or failed-login rate spikes immediately after deployment
A configuration or schema change in the release is identified as the trigger
title: Deployment Rollback Procedure

checks: Anchor on time: get the exact timestamp (and timezone) of one known failure
Search for ERROR and FATAL first, then the exception class name, around that timestamp
Find the correlation / request ID and follow it across services if present
Separate the first (root) error from repeated retry and knock-on errors
escalation: Escalate with evidence attached: timestamp, correlation ID, first error line, and the runbook you matched. Escalations with a log excerpt get answered faster.
steps: Collect: exact timestamp, user action, error text, and one full stack trace
Classify the top error: authentication, timeout, database, validation, or unknown
Match the classification to the runbook library (this assistant automates that match)
If the log shows a downstream timeout, switch to RB-103; a pool error, RB-105; an auth error, RB-101
Record what the log proved and what it did not — never guess past the evidence
symptoms: A problem is reported but the failing component is not yet known
You have an error message, a timestamp, or a stack trace and need a starting point
Multiple systems could be responsible and you need evidence before escalating
title: Log Triage — Reading Application Logs to Find the Failure

checks: Check queue depth and its trend over the last hour — growing, flat, or draining
Look for a poison message: the same message ID failing and redelivering
Check consumer thread count and whether all threads are stuck on one message
Verify the destination (document store, print service, mailbox) is accepting connections
escalation: Escalate to the integration team if the queue does not drain within 1 hour of removing a blocker, and to the destination vendor if their service is rejecting messages.
steps: If a poison message is identified, move it to the dead-letter queue per procedure and note its ID
Confirm the queue starts draining and monitor until depth returns to normal
If the destination is down, pause the consumer to stop retry churn and notify the destination's owner
After recovery, reconcile: count messages sent vs expected for the incident window
Record the poison message ID and payload reference for the owning team to fix the data
symptoms: Documents, letters, or outbound messages are generated late or not at all
Queue depth grows steadily while the consumer shows no errors
Source claims look correct — the delay is between systems
Restarting the consumer drains a few messages, then it stalls again
title: Message Queue Backlog — Asynchronous Integrations Stuck
